MOSCOW, Nov. 18.-Confront-
ed with stiff counterattacks, ad-
verse weather conditions and
difficult terrain, the Red Army
has yielded ground in the
Ukraine for the first time since
it began its successful offensive
four months ago.


The withdrawal was executed yes
terday in the Zhitomir- -Korostyshev
sector at the tip of the Red Army's
salient west of Kiev, and came on
the eve of the first anniversary of
the launching of the great Soviet
counteroffensive at Stalingrad on
November 18, 1912.


The retreat followed a series of
heavy Nazi counterattacks southeast
OF Zhltomlr an in the FaStov
sector, in which masses of tanks and
infantry were used in an attempt
to slice off the bulge in the Soviet
front. A Russian communique said
the drive cost the Germans $500
casualties and 80 tanks and troop
carriers.


(Advices from London said the


Germans were reported to have


thrown at least 10000 troops


into the Zhitomir counteras-


sault.)


Details Not Given.


The depth of the withdrawal was
not given in the Russian COM
munique, which confined itself to
the laconic report that the Red
Army. under enemy pressure, was
abandoning several settlements.


Moscow military observers, how
ever, believed the withdrawal was
not on a large scale, but was simply
a tactical maneuver designed to
prevent the encirclement of a COM
paratively small advance guard.


They explained that light mobile
column of tanks and motorized in
fantry had led the Russian drive
through Korostyshev and Zhitomir
and that the bulk Of the Red Army
forces was not able to maintain
the pace. Boggy ground impeded
troops movements and low visi-
bility restricted aerial activity, front
adviceS said.


Gen. Nikolai Vatutin's lst Ukrain-
ian Army. which carried out the re-
treat, has been one of the fastest
moving Russian units in the present
offensive, begun on July IL in the
Belgorod sector.


Other Forces Advance.


While the tip and left flank of the
Kiev salient sagged slightly under
the heavy enemy pressure, other Red
Army forces pushed forward on the
right flank toward the strategic rail
junction city of Korosten to the
north.


The Russians captured the towns
OF Narodichi, % miles northeast of
Korosten, and Chernobil, so miles
east OF Narodichi near the junction
OF the Pripet and Dnieper Rivers.
The German garrison in Korosten
was thus threatened from the south,
east and north but fought Stub
bornly to hold that valuable COM
munications and supply center, dis
patches said.


The width of the Kiev bridgehead,
however, left the Red Army with
ample space to adjust its positions
and to strike out anew from internal
lines against the scattered German
opposition.


On the lower White Russian front
to the north, Soviet columns were
fighting their way through the sub
urbs of Rechitsa, strongly fortified
city on the west bank of the
Dnieper, the communique said, and
had gained ground on the east bank
OF the river north of Gomel, tight
ening their grip on that beleaguered
stronghold.


New Drive Reported.


A new Soviet drive was also re-
ported under way near Arsha,
Dnieper River city 10 miles south
west of Smolensk, and the junction
point for the Leningrad-Od
Moscow Warsaw railway lines.


The Russians also were attacking
in the Southern Ukraine, continu-
ing their drive to clear out the
Dnieper bend. Here 1000 Germans
were reported killed, with 10 enemy
tanks, II guns and 48 trucks being
destroyed. Several important towns
were captured in a thrust toward
Krivoi Rog, the war bulletin said.


There was no mention of develop
ments in the battle for the Crimean
Peninsula, but dispatches from the
front indicated that fog and rain
were immobilizing both sides.

To say that Miss Beatrice

She not only works very day of

ALLIED HEADQUARTERS IN
NORTH AFRICA, Aug. 28.-The
steady Allied air scourging of
Southern Italy's railways has vir-
tually paralyzed train traffic
from the Naples area to the toe
and heel of the peninsula, air.
force officers declared today,
with fresh wreckage strewn yes
terday near Naples and by Flying
Fortresses at Sulmona, 100 miles
east of Rome.


Some trains are moving, but
with great difficulty and many de-
lays since main line tracks have
been knocked out in countless
places, switching stations and other
rail buildings demolished, and yards
filled with gaping craters, Allied
headquarters said.


Wrecked locomotives and passen-
ger and freight cars and in some
cases remains of entire trains
block the tracks at many points,
especially at Benevento, junction
near Naples where damaged freight
cars bar the way to the yards.


Freight Yards Blasted.


Other points hard hit by re-
lentless American day bombing
and British night hammering in
clude Naples, Villa Literna, Sapri,
laramie and Foggia.


Freight yards at Benevento were
straddled by bombs from United
States BIS Mitchells in renewed
attacks yesterday, and Flying Fort
resses in a heavy assault blasted
the lines at Sulmona near the east
coast for the first time. B-26 Ma
rauders hammered Caserta near
Naples, medium and fighter bomb
ers spread ruin wide over Southern
Italy. and RAF heavy Wellingtons
followed up last night with block
busters on the freight yards at
Salerno, south of Naples.


Twenty German and Italian fight
ers were downed as the enemy put
up stiffening resistance, and nine
Allied planes were lost yesterday


Aerial reconnaissance showed that
the line OF extremely heavy destruc-
ton extends across Italy from the
Gulf of Naples to the Gulf of Man
fredonia, and that rail traffic in all
the area south of this line is prac-
tically at standstill.


Troop Movements Slowed.


Spurs probably have been con-
structed around some main line
points where tracks were blown out,
enabling trains to pass, but greatly
slowing traffic. At other points, no
attempts have yet been made to re-
open the lines.


The rail paralysis undoubtedly has
made movements of troops and mill
tary supplies difficult problem for
the Axis, endangering defense of all
Southern Italy


Southern Italy's rail system con-
sists of main lines all along the coast
with an important east-west route
from Naples to the Adriatic coast
via Benevento and Foggia. There
are north and south inland lines
and many sidelines running through
Italy's innumerable valleys.


Scarcely any of them has escaped
Allied bombs, but the main juno
tion points haye been the chief
targets.


The onslaught on rail lines be-
gan August Is as Allied land forces
were closing in on Messina, making
few targets for the Air Force in
Sicily. 1t has been vigorously pur-
sued nearly every day since then.
and represents the most concen-
trated destruction of railways since
the start of the war.


Biggest Attack So Far.


Yesterdays program was the big
gest SO far in the number of freight
yards hit, and put the Northwest
Africa Tactical Air Force planes
out in their heaviest attacks since
Sicily fell.


These Tactical Force flights sent
four formations of Mitchells and
Bostons against the rail and road
hub of Catanzaro, Bostons to bomb
Axis gun positions at Reggie Gala
bria across from Messina, and A-36
Invaders to destroy rail junction
at Sibari and rake the west coast
ports of Paola and Cetraro.


The Mitchells laid bombs on the
locomotive works at Benevento be-
sides tearing up the rail lines, and
these flights, meeting the heaviest
opposition, shot down Is of the
days bag of enemy planes. One
formation alone tailed 13 of the
attackers.

heavy American bombers did a
swell job of smashing" targets at

ported excellent concentration" of

MIAMI. Fla, Jan. 13.-The gay
throng, celebrities and the cheering
were missing today-the day Hialeah
Park was scheduled to inagugrate its
glittering 46 days Of mid-winter rae
ing and set the Miami season in full
swing.


Hialeah didn't open, nor did Trop-
ical Park see any racing in the last
week of its fall season slated to close
yesterday. The ban on pleasure
driving served effectively to black
out horse racing here.


A year ago a fashionable crowd Of
1858 fans celebrated Hialeah's OPEN
ing by wagering $454,740. From the
race track they made rounds Of
night clubs and bright spots. Many
reached their hotels as the dawn
broke, slept through the day and
made ready for another night.


Now the best dressed people wear
khaki or navy blue. War factories
hum through the night, as places of
entertainment once did. The bright
lights have been snapped off under
dimout regulations. and a majority
of the luxurious hotels have been
stripped of their trappings and made
into barracks for soldiers and sailors.


Expensive cars with out-of-State
tags, commonplace a year ago, are
a curiosity this year. Traffic in gen.
eral has dwindled to a trickle of
private cars and bigger proportion
of busses, taxicabs and military
vehicles. Miamians are slow in TAX
ing to bicycles.


The dimout Of resort activities has
left two dog tracks and the Jai-Alai
fronton operating. Two other dog
tracks have closed. Only one-third
of the night clubs found in the area
a year ago are open now. Bars and
juke joints, on the other hand, have
increased and are doing land Office
business in beer, sandwiches and
canned music. Daytime streets are
crowded and few merchants COM
plain of lack Of trade.

MOSCOW, Nov. 27.-The army
newspaper Red Star said today
the Russians had crossed the
Berezina River, inflicting a new
blow on the disorganized Ger
man Army along the stream
where Napeoleon's legions met
final defeat during the retreat
from Moscow.


Following up his smashing victory
at Gomel, Gen. Constantin Rokos-
sovsky pushed through White Russia
west of the Dnieper River, outfank-
Ing the German base at Zhlobin, SO
miles northwest of captured Gomel,
the Army newspaper reported. The
railroad running southwest from
Zhlobin to Kalinkovichi was cut in
yesterdays westward surge, when
Soviet spearheads captured the town
of Shatsilki, where the railway
crosses the Berezina.


Gen. Rokossovskys White Russian
army reached the Berezina by
northward push along the west bank
Of the Dnieper, while other forces
enveloped and stormed the fortress
city OF Gomel east of the river.


Nazis Driven From Right Bank.


Red Star said a heavy artillery
barrage and repeated raids by the
Red Air Force drove the enemy
from the right bank of the Berezina,
which flows southeastward into the
Dnieper, 20 miles below Zhlobin.


Fast-moving advance spearheads
stormed into the towns of Nizhnia
and Olba, forming the strongest
knot of German resistance in this
sector. Then they famed out along
both banks of the Berezina, striking
north and northwest to sever the
zhlobin- n-Kalinkovichi railroad.


Red Star said the Germans still
were holding out in strongly forti-
fed bases along the Berezina to the
northwest and were offering stiff
resistance to the advancing Red
Army.


Gen. Rokossovskys triumph at
Gomel opened the way for a possible
general advance toward Pinsk and
Brest-Litovsk, chief cities of the
Polish Province of Polesie.


Siege Began October 13.


Gomel, last German-held bastion
east of the Dnieper River, fell yes
terday after siege which began
October 13, three weeks after the
Russians fought their way into the
Gomel sector and crossed the Sozh
River above the strongly fortified
Nazi base.


Held up for more than two months
by powerful German Notifications,
the Red Army troops, avoiding
costly frontal attacks against the
strategic stronghold, pushed west
from the Sozh in outflanking
maneuvers to the north and south.


Wednesdays breakthrough at
Propoisk, so miles north of Gomel,
completed the isolation of the be-
leaguered German garrison and de-
cided the outcome of the battle.


Today Gen. Rokossovsky's troops
were pouring through the Gomel
gap and extending their control on
the east bank of the Upper Dneiper.
Red Army advance guards already

which threatened to cut the escape
railway at Zhlobin Junction. Other
Soviet forces were cleaning up in
the Rechitsa area, west of Gomel.

Summer and solid military footing
find great and significant changes on the
central Russian front.


What is most important to the world
is the fact that there Is doubt about
whether the Russians or the Germans
will attack first. That the Russians
have become strong enough to mount a
summer offensive, without aid from
their old ally, General Winter, is de-
velopment OF major proportions.


Summer Of 1912 saw different pic
ture Then it was obvious that only the
Germans were strong enough to venture
an attack. with the Russians grimly on
Defense hoping for the early advent of
winter.


Now even the Germans admit that the
Russians are able to attack this summer.
This is automatic proof that the Red
Army has greatly augmented its mech.
anized equipment and can risk NUM-
tions and men in an offensive the while
reserving adequate forces and material
for defense.


Likely Spot for Drive.


All advices from both sides of the line
indicate that the central Russian front,
from Smolensk to Kharkov Is the like
liest site for the big push, whichever side
starts the great columns moving for
ward.


The front there is composed Of great
salients. In certain sectors, such as
Kharkov and Orel, the Nazis have the
advantage OF position. Near Kursk and
Smolensk the bulges in the line favor
the Russians.


The fighting OF the past few weeks, by
account of both sides. has been first
round sparring. The Russians must be
conceded an edge in the opening blows.
The salient 10 miles deep and 80 miles
wide driven into Nazi lines west of
Kursk threatens vital communications.


Underground sources on the continent,
reporting to refugee governments in
London. said the Germans had planned
their offensive to start last week, but
that Marshal Won Book hastily post
poned it when the Red push on Kursk
upset his supply plans.


The Russians have also made i'm
portant gains along the Mtensk-Zhiz-
dra line northwest of Orel. A Nazi push
aimed at Moscow from the Orel salient
must wait until these gains have been
won back.


New Tactics.


A tactic new to the Russian front. the
heavy bombing of key objectives behind
the lines has been increasingly evident
in dispatches from both sides. The
Germans raided Kursk and Cork in
force, while the Red aviation units have
consistently pounded rail functions and
supply dumps back of the German lines


The Reds have claimed air superiority
in the last MONTH augmenting the re-
port that United States lease-lend air.
craft in quantity is making its weight
felt In Russia.


Whatever develops. the fact that Rus
sia enters the summer season so strong
that Russian offensive is not only pos
sible but likely is happy augury for the
United Nations.

deadly fumes of "black damp" for
more than eight hours, stumbled and
craWled from their barricaded cell
last night as rescue parties freed
them.


Two other miners, who had joined
the barricaded group, became panic
stricken and dashed from their in
closure to death from carbon mon
oxide fumes 400 feet away.


The explosion thundered through
the East Tennessee soft coal mine
yesterday afternoon, rocking it from
tipple to the deepest seam.


Two miners who were almost out
side the mine tunnel when the blast
occurred were burned critically.
Three others in another section of
the mine escaped injury.

companions into an inclosure and
erected a cloth canvas barricade to
keep out the fumes.

Foreign Correspondent Of The Star and

WITH THE AMERICAN
FORCES IN NEW GUINEA, Jan.
6 Delayed Gen. Sir Thomas
Blamey, a member of the Allied
high command, inspected the
Buna battlefields and watched
bombers strike the Jap line Of
communications at Sanananda
today. While ground -strafing
planes peppered the lines, the
commander of the Allied land
forces, with the veteran Ameri-
can commander of the local front
at his side, paused in an Ameri-
can jeep to watch the renewal
of the air offensive against these
thoroughly intrenched and for
midable Jap positions.


After greeting the troops. Aus
tralian and American, encamped
under the shattered palms on the
ground they won. Gen. Blamey. who
wore an open-shirted Anzac blouse
and carried a shooting stick, speak
ing from experience in the Middle
East and Flanders said:


This is the most closely fortified
area 1 have ever known since
France. The troops who captured
emplacements like these did wond-
ers. 1t was the most terrific feat
ever to get here"


Paid Necessary Price.


Gen. Blamey said Dumas capture
has been not without cost.


TT was not cheap victory by any
means. But the price had to be
paid and the troops stood up to the
task and paid it,"


When asked to compare the per-
Torrance of the Inexperienced
Americans with the Tobruk veterans
with whom they shared three sal
tents and are still sharing the San
amanda front. Gen. Blamey said:


The Americans did their job. Our
men have had three years of war.
They got their experience the only
way it can be gained"


In one section of the marshy gov
eminent gardens, east of the bloody
triangle of Buna where the roads to
Buna village and Mission fork, bury
ing attachments were just locating
the bodies of Americans and Japs
who fell there as the Blamey party
reached the once sniper-sown
Quagm1re.


After surveying the tangle Of
pandanus, palm thicket and lawyers
vines with its chain OF pillboXes in
the taking of which the Americans
suffered considerable casualties, Gen.
Blamey said:


In this country every bump or
hollow may be bunker. There are
places where it is impossible to see
a yard ahead. The only way q man
can make cross country approach
is by going to his waist in sinking
mud"


Build Road Amid Mire.


Gen. Blamey and his party hiked
several hundred yards through the
heavy mud, flanked by water pools,
where American engineers includ-
ing many from MaSsa chusetts, were
standing in mud to their calves
building a corduroy road of giant
palmettos.


Gen. Blamey, who landed on the
American built airfleld, also in
spected the 13-ton Gen. Stuart
tanks which, manned by Austria
lians, crushed the Japs between the
Australian hammer and the Amer
lean anvil. He ate beef and
crackers at midday with the Amer
leans and took tea with the Aussie
tankmen.


AS the Australian commander re-
turned across Buna airfleld dark
column of smoke billowed up from
the Sanananda shore. 1t appeared
that our bombers had hit some OF
the Japs' storage dumps.


At one point several stray shots
from the partly Jap-held coast be-
tween Buna village and Sanananda
came near where Gen. Blamey stood,
but he was not harmed.


Engineers have found cunpingly
buried Jap artillery as well as air
craft sighting instruments, appar-
entity indicating the Japs hope to
return despite their defeat.

Almost at midnight, with the

In the wadi below the hill. a Brit
ish battery suddenly discovered 30

ported they lost only one tank.

came there were Is more wrecked
panzers abandoned in the little VAL

Hills.


Some German infantry still clung
to high ground. but were nearly sur
rounded by the British. All during
daylight today the enemy fought to
retreat from this unexpected trap

Back along the dusty road to the

ment with its name Hermann
Goering" on the sleeves Of their
disheveled uniforms.


I saw two of the abandoned Ger
man tanks towed into field repair

tain was creased by a wide smile as
he assured the world well have
them ready in no time to fight the
Boche."


Allied warplanes scared eastward
over this sector in scores of forma-
tions today in support Of the British
1st Army. Only once did the Ger
man fighter -bombers sneak through

umn of German motorized infantry

reported pushing on up the rail-

steppes toward Aleksandrovskoe, 80
miles farther north.

q considerable part OF what they

carded packing crates. The plant

day.

formed into labor companies under
their own officers since the armistice.
American experts supervise their
work.

Four Marine pilots flying Grammar Wild
cats have found they can fight Jap Zeros
without bullets.


After using all their ammunition to de-
stroy four Japanese dive bombers and dam
age three others which they found attack
ing an American naval force northwest of
Guadalcanal, the Wildcats still had to fight
their way home with empty guns.


They had flown only about fifteen miles
of their long trip back to Henderson Field
when Marine pilot spotted twelve Zeros.
The Japs didn't know that the Wildcat
guns were empty, but in spite of the odds
of three to one in their favor the Zeros
came in cautiously. AS each Zero dived at
an American plane, the Marine next in line
pulled up and faced the oncoming Japan
ese. The Jap didn't like seeing a Wildcats
nose coming straight at him and he'd pull
away. The bluff worked again and again
because from head-on tracer bullets aren't
visible and the Zeros thought they were
being fired on. The bluff worked too be-
cause in other engagements the Japs had
found that they couldn't trade lead on even
terms with Wildcat. The fight continued
to within two miles of Henderson Field.
The Wildcats were shot up plenty-one Of
them had twenty bullet holes-but they all
came home.


Those boys are members of one of the
fabulous Marine outfits whose Pratt & Whit
ney-powered Wildcats have kept the air over
Guadalcanal clear Of enemy planes. On one
day alone their squadron sent thirty Zeros,
two destroyers, and two cargo ships to their
ancestors

Increasing horsepowers and higher alti-
tudes of operation set up ever more difficult
propeller problems. Hamilton Standard engi-
neers are meeting this challenge in several
distinct and separate ways. They are already
testing propellers which will handle horse
powers far above today's maximum Report
ers were allowed to see some of these devel-
opments, but for reasons of national security
no word of them can be published.
+ Guests gasped as Grammar Wildcat
and the new Vought Corsair streaked across
the field in speed runs to demonstrate
secret development which makes the planes
fairly jump through the sky and climb like
frightened angels.

Together the three divisions met the three
main equirements-speed speed and more
speed. One of the cleanest airplanes in serv-
ice, the skin is entirely spot welded and flush
riveted to eliminate resistance by tiny rivet
heads. Even air scoops have been built into
the wing.


Adding to its graceful lines is the distinc-
tive gull wing, developed naturally as the
design progressed. The enormous horse
power called for an exceptionally large pro-
peller, necessitating extra height from which
to swing clear of the carrier deck. The gull
wing solved this problem, and at the same
time permitted the wing to spring from
the round fuselage at right angles, giving
maximum aerodynamic efficiency.

days ago.


Field Marshal Guenther Won
Kluge,s armored columns also were
smashing with fresh emphasis on
the Orel-Kursk end of the Kursk
salient, but here, too, the Russians
claim, they were absorbing the best
that the Nazis could give.


The Kursk sector blazed into more

of the German offensive began, but
1t was not yet clear whether Mar
shall Won Kluge has shifted the main
weight of his attack from Belgorod
in a possible search for an easier
spot to breach the unyielding Rus
sian lines.

"a German communiQue,

(The communique claimed

clared that the Germans were

Tigers. Red Army artillery and
aviation protecting the Red infantry

remainder, the Russians said.

through in the Belgorod area, the
Germans attacked strongly in the
Orel-Kursk sector at the northern
end of the Kursk salient.

of infantry attacked on one narrow
sector. The Russians reported many
tanks destroyed and more than 1000
men killed. At another position on

offensive are constantly being re-
inforced and the Red artillery which

them of as fast as they come.

CHICAGO. June 1.-THE mighty

President Edwin Barclay of Liberia


When he landed in the New Worlo


at the Brazilian port of Natal. he


was met by President Getulio Vargas


Few sharper contrasts could be


imagined than those two meetings
between chief executives. Liberia is
a small Negro republic founded 12l
| years ago by freed American slaves
| The descendants of those freedmen
are the ruling class in Liberia, hav-
ing preserved American traditions,
and the little republic has always
had the benevolent interest of the
United States. When America en-
tered the war, Liberia followed its
example and became a useful air
base on the West African coast. Its
strategic Importance has somewhat
diminished since the rallying of all
French Africa to the Allied side, but
it retains its economic significance
as the seat of rubber plantations
established a decade ago by Ameri-
can interests and now coming into
large-scale production.


The Liberian visit may be classed
as gracious episode. More impor-
tant was the conference between
Presidents Roosevelt and Vargas.
Natal itself has high strategic value,
situated as it is at the easternmost
tip of the Brazilian hump" which
juts out toward the corresponding
West African bulge. Across the rela-
lively slender waist of the Atlantic
Ocean fly streams of passenger,
transport and bomber planes, the
vital air link between the New and
Old Worlds. Natal is likewise the
chief base of the joint Brazilian and
American aerial patrol which seeks
to combate the depredations of Axis
submarines. The South Atlantic
Ocean is perhaps the most danger
GUS region for Allied merchant ship
ping. 1t is certainly the most vexa-
. tious problem for Allied anti-subma-
rine strategy, because its vast spaces
and the multiplicity of sea routes
there render adequate convoy and
patrol extremely difficult. The prob
lem's urgency is high lighted by a
news release simultaneously with the
disclosure of the Roosevelt-Vargas
meeting that five ships out of an
American convoy had been sunk by
U-boats in a daring night attack off
the South American coast.


Discussion of the submarine men
ace doubtless was a leading topic in
the Natal conference. Brazil GER
tainly has been doing yeoman service
in this, as in other respects, since its
entry into the war against the Axis
powers. With our assistance, chain
of. airfields has been built all along
the Brazilian coast. and the rapidly
expanded Brazilian air force already
has accounted for several Axis sub
marines. The potential strength of
this biggest American republic,
larger than the continental United
States and with incalculable natural
resources, is very great and is being
effectively modified for the common
cause. The cordial understanding
already evolved between the two ma
tions will surely be promoted and
intensified by the conversations be-
tween their chief executives. From
every aspect, the Natal meeting
should bear good fruit.

INDIANAPOLIS, May 18.-One
of the worst floods since the dis
astrous waters of 1913 tore
through Central and Northern
Indiana today


At least four lives have been lost
in the raging torrents. More than
500 families have been moved from
flooded homes in Marion, Frankfort,
Wabash, Indianapolis and other
places.


Flood waters Surged over thou
sands of acres of lowlands, dam
aging early planted farm crops.
Numerous victory gardens have been
washed away.


Nine blocks of sandbagged levee
and the Charles Mills Dam at Ma
rion ouivered under the pressure of
swollen Mississenewa River Three
hundred families in the area were
evacuated. ..


Police at Frankfort moved $50
families from their homes although
the city isn't even near a river. A
drainage ditch running through part
of the town couldn't cope with the
heavy flow of water.


The Wabash River at Wabash
reached 9 feet over flood stage
and was still raging. Seventy five
homes were cleared there.


A bridge was torn loose at Logans-
port. A dam on Big Eagle Creek
gave way northwest of Indianapolis
and war plant workers living west
of the city were told to stay home
until the waters had subsided.


The local Weather Bureau warned
residents along the lower Wabash
and the West Fork of White River
to expect rapid rising of the streams
with serious floods.

battle for the Kokoda track, through

In many ways the tennis map
covers more sporting terrain than
any other sport. The Davis Cup
and national championships have
been won by the United States,
Great Britain, France, Australia and
New Zealand. where Germany had
an outstanding star in Won Cramm.


Now Ecuador offers South Amer

of Francisco Segura who will be
extremely hard to surround and cut
down when the United States tennis
championship opens at Forest Hills.


This will be South Americas first
big chance to enter the long parade
that has come from a large portion
of the scrapping planet.


The strongest bids that have come
from South America so far were the
Argentina polo team and more than
one soccer outfit that has scrambled
to the top. Argentina's polo crop
In other years always was good, but
Ecuador now remains the only South
American country with a national
championship in sight.

many tennis stars the United

ston. Richards, Vines and Bulge

Wilding, Crawford and strong
young colony, checked by the war.

with Lacoste, Cochet and Borotra-
not overlooking Suzanne Lenglen.

man while Kumagae and Shimidzu

bledon in a way has been the tennis
capital.

1914, just a few days after the Ger

knew he never would be back again
as he felt that quick and certain
death was to be his part.

a few months later. There has been
no finer sportsman.

l1lden was the greatest tennis
player of them all-at his peak
T1lden came to the front in 1920
when he and Bill Johnston brought
back the Davis Cup from Australia.
where 1t still is waiting for some
challenger after this war is over.


11lden almost was unbeatable for
the next five years. Big Bill has
been a star for more than 20 years,
the most colorful figure that ever
came to any court.


He had speed and power with an
amazing amount of generalship and
for some Is years was in more big
matches than any other two men.


When the 1943 title whirl opens

sign Fred Schroeder, the cham

berg, Sidney Wood, Bitsy Grant

bring him down at Forest Hills
when the next show opens. but
there are sounder bets the other
way. Young Bob Falkenberg Is no

jungle plateau from which Japa-
nese had overlooked the New
Guinea sector where the most
important invasion of the South
west Pacific is possible was in
Gen. Douglas MacArthur's hands
today.


Australians who had followed
closely behind 26-ton tanks as far as
the tanks could crash their way
through the dense growth stormed
those heights yesterday at Sattel-
berg, slaughtered the Japs in their
dugouts, drove survivors in fight
along trail to, the north and seized
the field guns and military equip
ment they abandoned.


Sattelberg, first major enemy posi-

miles to the southeast, looks down
on the Huon Gulf, where Gen. Mac
Arthur's ground troops are separated
only by the narrow waters of Dam
pier Strait from Westen New Brit
ain. Loss of New Britain would tear
apart Japan's entire South and
Southwest Pacific position inasmuch
as Eabaul harbors the warShips and
planes for the defense of the sec
tor-New Guinea. New Britain, New
ireland and the Northern Solomons.


Accomplished by Hard Fighting.


The capture OF Sattelberg> nine
days after the drive opened from
near Finschhafen was a feat accom-
plished by hard fighting, deadly ac-
curate air attacks and the brilliant
work of American engineers in
keeping the supplies moving.


So difficult and treacherous was
the battle-ground that today's COM
munique paid this tribute:


In this gallant attack, the most
difficult operational conditions due
to mountainous jungle terrain were
encountered and overcome"


The frantic defenders broke for
the Wareo trail into the northern
jungles after three forces of Aussies,
moving in from as many directions,
threatened them with encirclement.

Nineteenth century American
military prints on sheet music COM
pose the current special exhibition
of the Division of Graphic Arts,
United States National Museum, in
its new gallery in the Smithsonian
Building. These prints, lent by two
Washington collectors, Miss Edith
A. Wright and Miss Josephine Nc
Dewitt, are examples of a type
almost unknown to the public to-
day; yet a century ago they were
familiar and popular form of art.


Many of our cities Gncluding
Washington used to- have one or
more military organizations: Light
guards, volunteers and zouaves.
They wore colorful uniforms, those
of each city group having distinctive
character and accoutrements. Rep
resentations of these various COM
panieS, and sometimes of individual
officers, were made by outstanding
lithographers of the period to adorn
the covers of missionaries,
dances, etc, often dedicated to
the respective organizations. Uong-
time Washingtonians may remem-
ber that Sousa wrote march
for our National Fencibles at
somewhat later period than that
covered by these prints: 1835-1870)


Pendleton, Moore, Thayer, Buff
ford, Endicott, Duval and Sarony
are the artists whose work is in the
present collection, which represents
Is cities; Albany, Baltimore, Boston,
Brooklyn, Charleston, Chicago, Du-
buque, Hartford, Lexington, Louis
Vile, Milwaukee, New York, Phila-
delphia, Providence and Savannah.


There is much more variety than
one would expect to find, not only in
the uniforms but also in the groups
of these sheet music Autographs.
More than half of them are printed
in several colors, and in some in
stances gold. Gazing upon the gor-
geous plunage affected by our great
grandfathers when soldering, we
are bound to conclude that military
life had pleasure and even dash of
glamour, which the two appalling
wars of this century have COM
pletely destroyed.


The New York City Guard, for
instance, wore scarlet coats, tight
dark blue trousers and tall fur caps;
their portrait will remind many
people of London's Horse Guards
uniforms and lofty BUSHES. The
Albany Burgesses' Corps had uni
forms somewhat similar to New
York's. Brooklyn's Light Guard was
resplendent in black and silver,
white trousers and red sashes, with
towering shakos heavily bedecked.
The United States Zouave Cadets of
Chicago must have looked like
Turks, with their baggy trousers,
short jackets, richly trimmed blouses
and fezes.


Some of these Autographs have
scenic backgrounds typical of the
locales of the respective military
organizations. The harbor of
Charleston, S. C. appears behind
the Jasper Guards of that city; thesI
New England Guards are deploying
before the Boston State House; the
west Point Dream Waltz" depicts
cadets with ladies before a large
hotel overlooking the Hudson. An
other group is portrayed at a BAN
quet table, heavily laden with fruit
and wine.

could be enlarged to include colored

LONDON, Sept. 13.-A veil of
wartime secrecy was lifted today
from the Arctic isle of Spitsbergen
and the Norwegian government-in-
exile told for the first time the story
of small band of Norwegians who
maintained a vital weather station
there for year and half.


The government disclosed that no
word had been heard from the gar
rison since it signaled the APPROACH
of a German feet which Berlin
announced had attacked and de-
stroyed installations there last We'd
nesday.


Since May, 1912, the garrison,
numbering fewer than 100 men, had
manned the weather station and
provided information needed for
ships sailing the northern route to
Russia.


The last official news concerning
the archipelago. only $50 miles be-
low the North Pole, was announced
in September, l941, when an Allied
force evacuated all persons living
there and destroyed coal mines
which the Germans were reported
using. Then tight censorship was
clamped down.


A month after the Allied landing,
the Germans moved in. The fol-
lowing May the Norwegians arrived
to build an Allied weather station.
German aircraft attacked the group
daily. On July British naval
force arrived, and the German gar
rison slipped away.


Since then, the Norwegians had
been undisturbed until the German
warships arrived.

MOSCOW, Dec. 8-One of the
most desperate German tank and
infantry assaults launched during
the seven-week battle for the Kiev
bulge has forced the Red Army to
retire from several towns in the
Chernyakhov-Zor area, but
Soviet troops have scored important
gains southwest of Kremenchug and
almost completely enveloped Zna-
menka. vital rail junction in the
Dnieper bend, a Russian war bull
letin said today.


Russian advices said approx
mately 1,700 tanks had been hurled
into a narrow sector west of Kiev
by Field Marshal Fritz Won Mann
stein. The Russian communique
said the Nazis had lost SO of their
tanks and left at least 1900 dead on
the field of battle.


Russians Gain in South.


The Nazi gains in the Kiev bulge
however, were offset by Russian
gains to the south. Here three
Red Army columns were driving on
Znamenka from separate directions
and one already was within four
miles of the towns gates. the COM
munique indicated. Fall of this
strategic rail junction, which front
dispatches said was apparently in
evitable, would tend to disrupt the
whole German communications and
supply system in the vast area be-
low Kiev and would undoubtedly
help to relieve enemy pressure on
the Kiev salient.


Sixteen German strongholds fell
before the Soviet advance below
Kremenchug, the communique re-
ported. One of them was the rail-
road station of Pantavevka, 10 miles
southeast of Znamenka, marking a
l2-mile gain along the railroad from
AleXandrlya. Two of the four rail
lines serving Znamenka have now
been severed, leaving only the routes
south to Nikolaev and southwest to
Kirovograd in Nazi possession. The
rail towns of Tsibulevo, IA miles
northwest, and Dimitrovka. 7>miles
northwest, were captured in Tues
days opening drive in this sector.


Reds Seize Three Supply Trains.


The Russians counted more than
1000 dead Germans on the blizzard
swept approaches to Znamenka
after yesterdays fighting. "A con-
siderable number" of prisoners were
taken, while three railroad trains
complete with supplies fell into
Soviet hands. Seventy-fve enemy
tanks were wrecked-a total of l2s
for the day, the communique an
nounced.


With the battle for Znamenka
reaching a decision, front dispatches
pointed out that the Soviet armies
under Gen. Rodion Y. Malinovsky
were now less than 140 miles from
the Odessa-Lwow railway to the
west, key to all German communica-
tions in the Ukraine. Krivoi Rog.
enemy-held manganese center
southeast of znamenka, loomed as
an early objective on the Red Army
schedule.

ference last night.

end today to the spectacular activi-
ties of Hugh McAteer, Irish rebel
leader who slid down rope of bed
sheets to escape from Belfast
prison last January after serving
two months of a 15-year sentence
for treason.

him into house, and found him
sitting in the kitchen, where he said
amicably, "Okay, boys, guess it's
over"


McAteer was the young revolu-
tionary who once warned the United
States that American troops in
Northern Ireland certainly would
become involved in a resumption
of hostilities between Ireland and
Great Britain"


Last April, with a $4,000 price on
his head, he and three heavily
armed companions walked into a
Belfast movie, stopped the show
and conducted memorial services
honoring "the men who have died
for Ireland"

By the Associated Press.


For the third time in two days
American Liberators have at
tackled Mill Atoll in the Southern
Marshall Islands, 800 miles
northwest of the recently con-
quered Gilberts. They shot
down 4 and possibly 7 of 20 in
tercepting Zeros in the action
Thursday, which was reported by
Admiral Chester w. Nimitz at
Pearl Harbor last night.


This was twice the number of in
terceptors met the day before, in
dicating the Japanese are ferrying
planes into the Marshalls to replace
their steady losses to the Liberators
and to meet an expected amphibious
invasion from the Gilberts, II these
requirements are coming over the
usual supply route via Wake, it would
indicate that other enemy fortresses
farther north in the Marshalls have
also been reinforced.


Japanese similarly showed greater
air strength in New Guinea, causing
damage Thursday in the Ramu
Valley, where Australians resumed
their advance toward Madang earlier
in the week. Other Aussies pushed
deeper into the Huon Peninsula
jungle beyond recently captured
Wareo, Gen. Douglass Macarthur
announced at his Southwest Pacific
headquarters.


Cape Gloucester Bombed.


For the twelfth straight day Allied
heavy bombers blasted Cape Glou-
cester. potential invasion point of
New Britain, across narrow Dampier
Strait from the Huon Peninsula. PIT
boats sank 10 enemy supply barges
on the Huon coast while a Navy
Catalina sank a freighter off New
Ireland, presumably on its way to
supply the once powerful fortress
of Rabaul, New Britain.


Mill and Jaluit Atolls, key jap
anese outposts, were bombed twice
on Wednesday. In the latest at
tack the Liberators dropped IS tons
Of bombs.


All the United States Army planes
returned to their equatorial base,
despite the Japanese fighters at
tempt to bring them down with
aerial bombs, machine guns and
cannon. All six aerial bombs the
japanese used missed their targets.
Some American airmen were wound
ed and part of the bomber con-
tingent was slightly damaged.


On the previous day the Liberators
returned with slight damage and
one wounded man after shooting
down two Of the 10 interceptors.


Admiral Nimitz did not report the
damage done to Mill on either day.


Mill, like other key points in the
Marshalls, was bombed almost daily
preceding the American invasion of
the Gilbert Islands, south of the
Marshalls. American carrier borne
planes made a devastating raid on
the Marshalls last Saturday.


Australian patrols swept aside
light enemy resistance along the
coast of New Guinea and inland
from Wareo Thursday and Friday,
further extending their grip on
Huon Peninsula.


Killed I'll Japs.


Advancing over high ground
Thursday, one Australian unit cap
tured Bazuluo Village, a mile and
a half due west of Wareo. In the
coastal sector their comrades killed
81 japanese in patrol clashes.


Through the activity of their
patrols the Australians were able to
push their outposts from a quarter
Of a mile to a mile and a quarter
farther northwestward along the
coast.


An unspecif1ed number of Japa-
nese planes raided Allied positions
in the Dumpu area of the Ramu
Valley early Friday, causing minor
damage and casualties. There were
patrol clashes but no material
change in the ground situation.


In the Solomons sector bad
weather was reported for the third
straight day, affording japanese
engineers opportunity to get bombed
out Bougainville airfields in opera
ton for use against the American
beachhead at Empress Augusta Bay.

Associated Press War Correspondent.


MOSCOW, March 27.-Two VIM
some, bright-eyed Red Army sniper
girls, Natalia Kovsheva and Maria
Polivanova, have been awarded the
highest of Russian honors, the Hero
of the Soviet Union award-but
posthumously.


The girls went to school together
and worked together. They went TO
the front together. And they died
together.


When the workers battalion was
formed in Moscow in October, 194l.
as the Germans hammered their
way toward the capital, the young
girls left school one morning and
applied for posts.


I'VE want to be fighters" said
Natalia.


I'VE want to carry guns said
Maria.


The commissar looked them I'D
and down and shook his head. They
appeared too delicate for the rigors
of the bitter Russian front. The
girls pleaded. Finally the commits
sar gave in.


Soon Natalia and Maria were on
their way to the front-with their
guns.


Pick Off Sc in ST, Days.


During their first six DAYS of
sniping, they picked off 36 of the
enemy. They marched with the
men on Skis and endured all the
hardships Of the soldiers life. When
their total killed reached 300, they
are awarded the Order of the Red
Star.


Inseparable friends, they partici-
pated in the heaviest action as the
Germans surged forward. In a
sharp battle the group with which
they fought held off the Nazis for
a long time, but at last there were
only three fighters, the two girls and
a man, Ivan Novikov.


All three were wounded. Their
bullets finally gave out. The Ger
mans charged. The girls threw two
hand grenades. driving the Ger
mans off momentarily. But on they
came.


Then the grenades gave out.


These courageous daughters of

SAN FRANCISCO, April 13.-
A desperate attempt of four con-
victS to escape from the island
fortress prison of Alcatraz re-
suited today in the reported
deaths of two, the recapture of a
third and the disappearance of
the fourth.


The man recaptured was Harold
Martin Brest, desperate bank robber,
serving a life term.


The four overpoWered and bound
and gagged two guards and leaped
into San Francisco Bay from the
island prison.


Warden j. A. Johnston said that
when the prison launch drew along
side Brest, he was holding James A.
Boarman, Indianapolis bank robber,
who had been shot by guards who
fired from the prison towers.


He let 60 of Boarman and the
convict sank beneath the waves
His body was not recovered.


Another Shot browns.


Indications were, Warden john
ston said, that Floyd Hamilton the
third man, was shot and drowned
The fourth man. Fred Hunter, 43,
Cleveland, was unaccounted for.


Warden Johnston said Hunter
and Boarman carried prison-mad
knives. They and the other two
first encountered a custodial officer.
overpowered him, then attacked
Henry Weinhold, captain of the
guards, and bound, tied and gagged
both men,


Then the four leaped from VIM
dow and headed for the beach
around the rocky island.


Meanwhile Weinhold slipped his
bonds and reached police whistle
to sound the alarm. Almost simul-
taneously guards In the surrounding
towers poured out rifle fire.


Boarman was shot, either as he
fed into the bay, or as he tried to
swim to freedom. When the prison
boat drew alongside of Brest, Penn
sylvania bank robber and kidnaper,
he was holding Boarman up in the
water AS he loosed his hold. Boar
man slipped under. His body was
not found.


Break Worst at Prison.


Today's sensational break, the
worst the prison had experienced
since it was made virtual fortress
for incarceration of the Nations
worst criminals, occurred about
1925 am.


Brest was one of the only two
convicts to win release from Alca-
traz by habeas corpus, but he wasn't
out long. He was originally sem
fenced in 1887 to 25 years for rob-
bing the First National Bank of
Volant. Pa. In February, 1899, he
won his release on grounds he wasn't
represented by counsel at his trial
He promptly was re-arreSted, tried
in Pittsburgh for bank robbery and
kidnapping, and received new sem
tences of life imprisonment plus
IS years.


Hamilton, 36. of Dallas, was SEN
fenced in November, 1888. at Fort
Smith, Ark, for violating the bank
robbery and motor vehicle theft laws
and for assault. He was serving 80
years.


Hunter. 43, was sentenced at Cleve-
land to 25 years for assault and con-
spiracy to harbor Alvin Karpis while
the latter was being hunted for kid
naping.


No Break Ever Successful.


There had been no record of a
successful attempt to escape from
the rockbound island prison.


The prisoners making the break
today used the same method en-
ployed by two men who disappeared
from the island fortress. The men,
Ralph Roe and Ted Cole, swan
away from the rock in 1887. during
heavy fog and may have reached
shore safely. But prison author
,ities generally believe that the
strong currents and cold water
brought them death.

The War Shipping Administrator
is drafting revised form for its
standard ship charter contract in
order to effect economies in wartime
operation of the merchant marine.
VISA officials said today.


The new charter contract. which
will replace outstanding contracts
as they expire. combines features
of the standard time-charter form
and the standard bare-boat charter
form, and it was explained, inclines
toward the bare-boat form.


Under a time -charter form, the
VISA, as charterer, pays fat fee
for vessels services on a monthly
basis, with actual operation and
management left in the hands of the
owners who pay all operation and
management costs.


Under the bare-boat form, the
vessel Is turned over completely to
the VISA which provides its own
crews and pays other operating and
management costs In addition to the
fee paid the owners.


Present charter contracts follow
the time charter plan generally.


VISA officials said the new form
is being worked out in negotiations
with shipowner representatives.

Selective service headquarters now
is polling draft boards to find out
how many available single and child
less married men are left through
out the country.


They will match that information
against the October calls of the
armed forces-not yet received-to
find out if they have enough men to
fill October calls without drafting
prewar fathers.


Until they get those two sets OF
f1gures-the ones from the draft
boards and the ones from the armed
forces-neither Selective Service Di-
rector Hershey nor War Manpower
Chairman McNutt can predict what
day the first prewar fathers will 60
into uniform.


Estimates Changed Little.


Only the military knows how many
men it will need for the rest of the
year Despite military successes
and fewer casualties than expected,
however, calls of the armed forces
have veered little from estimates
presented to the War Manpower
Commission at the beginning of the
year.


The Army has told VINO that
there were certain "imponderables
that would have to be taken into
consideration, but so far these i'm
ponderables' haven't made much
difference in draft calls-either to
increase or reduce them.


The requirements of the armed
forces usually are presented to
selective service two months in ad-
vance. BY the middle of this
month, therefore, selective service
officials will know what the armed
forces want them to procure.


Await Draft Board Reports.


Reports from the draft boards will
clear up the second unknown
whether or not there are enough
single and childless married men to
fill the October call.


Recently, selective service
spokesman reported there were
enough single and childless married
men to fill calls through September.
There may be some left over. How
many. nobody knows. That de-
pends on how many of the men
figured as available will pass the
physical examinations, how many
will take appeals, how many will be
granted temporary stays of induc-
ton, how many will wind up with
occupational deferments.


1t has been indicated already that
the division Of single and childless
married men throughout the States
Is uneven. A survey last week showed
that some States figured they would
not have to take fathers until De-
cember, If calls continued at the
same level. Other States said they
had already reached the bottom of
the barrel"


Readjustment Promised.


Selective service has now promised
to readjust the calls on the basis of
these new figures. The States that
figured they could hold out till De-
cember will get heavier calls. The
bottom of the barrel" States will
get light calls.


That means that fathers will be
called earlier in the States that
thought they could hold out and
later in the States that had ex-
hausted their pools, but the call will
be simultaneous in all States.


Whether the leveling out process
will prevent the drafting of fathers
in October-or delay 1t even two
weeks-is a question that neither
Gen. Hershey nor Mr.. McNutt can
answer till they see what the armed
forces say they must have.

Last night aircraft of the bomber

The Italian naval base at Spezia

naissance flights over Western Ger

Three bombers are missing"

ascertained." The high command
communique. broadcast from Rome,

Milan.


The defenses, though clearly
strengthened, were no more effec-

nouncement said.


The raid on Spezia was the first
of the war for that fortified city, the
site of artillery works and establish
ments for the production of elec-
trical supplies and marine weapons,
especially torpedoes. .....s


Last nights attacks were the RAF,s
third successive night foray over
Europe and followed a day during
which United States Army bombers
struck at Northwest Germany in
the second all-American daylight
assault on the Reich.

England during the night and four
NaZi planes machine -gunned q

ualties.


Large formations Of Flying Fort
resses participated in the daylight

bombing by the RAF.


Swarms Of German fighters in

GIA, July Is Delayed. The
fight for Laiana beach today was
like this: Our tanks went down
the line as the Japanese pill
boxes were discovered. There
were men on each side of each
tank. They fired at the pill
boxes with automatic rifles and
the tanks followed with their fire
from guns which the men using
them call sweet baby cannon" :"


After them our infantry, inching
along under fire from snipers in the
trees. sometimes crawling, sometimes
running in crouch from cover and
leaving other infantrymen coming up
from the lear to kill the sripers,
went toward the pillboxes with
grenades and fixed bayonets to make
sure every Jap in them was dead.


The fight was small but of great
The success of it gave us beach,
head only 2 miles from the Jap air
port at Munda, and also preached
the outer line of the last Jap de-
fenses in New Georgia Most i'm
portant, however, was securing the
new beachhead which cuts our sup
ply lines by more than two-thirds.


Supply Problem Acute.


I'VE had been using many of our
combat troops here to carry supplies
on their backs because of the clut-
tered nature of the terrain. Now
most of these men can be released
to fight the enemy instead of the
mud and jungles.


The fight was interesting, too. be-
cause this was the first time tanks
had been used successfully in the
thick jungle. The Japs tried to at
tack with IA tanks in the Guadal-
canal jungle last October, lost 13 of
them and never used tanks again
When I left the front lines this
afternoon, with the attack well over,
we had not lost single tank.


And for the troops here the fight
will-o'-the-w -wisp nightmare of the
last II days. The enemy had stop
ped his rear-guard action and was
making stand at last, evidently
because it was impossible for him to
retreat further without imperiling
his position here.


The fact that there was, at last.
an enemy whose throat could be
taken in the two hands and
strangled gave us, watching from the
back areas. sense of relief so great
it amounted to JOY, and the feeling
extended In some measure even to
the front lines.


The advance Yesterday had
caught the enemy in an arc. This
arc ran generally from the south
to the northwest, with the enemy
in it anchored strongly to the beach
and holdind a ridge while we held
ravine beneath it. This morning
troops on top of the loop of the
arc began working south toward the
beach while the rest of the arc
moved toward the west.


A half hour heavy artillery bar
rage and bombing preceded our
attack, but the "softening up pro-
cess" had not dented the enemys
crust. The artillery in World War
I would destroy deeply imbedded
positions only with the greatest
difficulty and even when they could

BY The Associated Press.


LONDON. April 1.-Two enemy
submarines were sunk last month
by the Fighting French corvette
Aconit in an Atlantic convoy battle
in which the relatively new British
destroyer Harvester was lost, the
Admiralty announced today.


Near midnight the 1,34O-ton
Harvester located a U-boat and
brought her to the surface with
depth charges and then rammed
her, the Admiralty said The sub
marine became jammed under the
Harvester's stern and remained
fast for several minutes before
breaking clear.


The corvette sighted the U-boat
on the surface and engaged her
with gunfre and finally rammed
her amidships sinking the raider
Immediately, the communique re-
ported.


The Harvester's damage was such
that she could proceed only at very
SLOW speed, but the commander, A.
A. TAFT, ordered the corvette to re-
turn to the CONVOY. which still was
in danger of attack.


Later, the Admiralty said, the
Harvester was forced to stop and
was torpedoed and sunk while lying
still.


The Aconit came back to pick up
the destroyer's survivors and spotted
another U-boat on the surface.


Again the corvette depth charged,
and finally rammed the second
raider and sank her.


Harvester survivors had the Salts
faction of seeing the second subma-
rine 60 to the bottom, The Har-

persons.

gunned a crowded London-bound

hurt.

ed away for several minutes before
